A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DRAKES research. The main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original computational experiments on enhancer design and protein inverse folding, including reward-oracle evaluations, baseline comparisons and protein-energy simulations.

after.justification: v2 retains the original biological experiments and adds optimization ablations, protein confidence and diversity evaluations, and toxicity-controlled text-generation results.

M1.justification: The fixed-mask DRAKES algorithm, Gumbel-Softmax backpropagation and trajectory KL objective are retained. Appendix D adds an extension for stochastic initialization: jointly optimize the initial distribution and generator, with an additional KL penalty on the initial distribution. This is a limited methodological extension, not a replacement of the experimentally used algorithm.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates regulatory DNA design and protein inverse folding. v2 Appendix F.4 adds toxicity-controlled natural-language generation using an OpenWebText-pretrained masked diffusion model, substantially broadening the evaluated domain and task. The biological datasets and tasks remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The existing biological comparisons retain Pretrained, CG, SMC, TDS, CFG and DRAKES without KL; the PDB comparison still includes ProteinMPNN. The new text experiment reuses Pretrained, CG, SMC and TDS. No new comparator is introduced or removed from a matched experiment.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce truncation sweeps and constant-versus-linear temperature schedules, protein sequence entropy, and an alternative success criterion combining Pred-ddG > 0 with pLDDT > 80. The text protocol uses 20-token outputs, 20 diffusion steps, 100 fine-tuning updates and 320 evaluation samples per method. Existing biological splits and main-table settings are retained; App-Log-Lik merely renames the existing ELBO-based metric.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained KL ablation and oracle checks, v2 Tables 4, 5, 10 and 11 test sensitivity to gradient truncation and temperature scheduling in both biological tasks. Tables 12 and 13 add protein-confidence and sequence-diversity analyses, testing whether the reported advantages persist under another structural criterion and coexist with diverse outputs.

E5.justification: Both versions report biological comparisons using means and standard deviations across three random seeds. v2 explicitly reuses this practice for the new pLDDT comparison. No increase in repeated runs, new confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: The original main Tables 1–2 and matched appendix results remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial new results. These include DRAKES's pLDDT-based success rate of 72.3%, protein entropy of 33.3 versus 34.7 for Pretrained, and mean text Pred-Score of 10.044 versus 9.817 for TDS. New truncation and schedule tables also report performance under alternative settings.

T1.justification: v1's terminal-distribution guarantee assumes a deterministic initial state. v2 Appendix D adds a modified control problem and proof covering learned stochastic initial distributions, deriving an optimal initial law proportional to exp(V0/alpha) times the original initial law. This substantially extends the guarantee's scope while retaining the original main theorems and proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: KL-regularized reward optimization for discrete diffusion, differentiable Gumbel-Softmax backpropagation, a theoretical characterization, and demonstrations in DNA and protein design. The additional experiments support these contributions without redefining the main claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains intermediate truncation as a balance between updating early sampling stages and memory/optimization difficulties, and interprets the entropy results as preserving diversity alongside stability. These are substantive additional interpretations. The differentiable-reward limitation and existing discussion of reward over-optimization are retained.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses use of one NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU and base Gumbel temperatures of 1.0 for DNA and 0.5 for proteins. It documents the text models and fine-tuning recipe and adds a reproducibility statement referring to code and data at the already cited repository. The biological temperature disclosures do not establish changed settings.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantive comparison with Venkatraman et al.'s relative trajectory balance and citations supporting stochastic initialization, continuous-domain optimization, Concrete relaxation and the text experiment. The existing guidance/RL/classifier-free positioning is retained. The Dirichlet-diffusion discussion moves to Appendix A rather than being removed.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 refines theorem explanations and terminology, changes author/correspondence information, adds reproducibility and acknowledgement sections, and reorganizes the appendices. These are localized editorial and structural changes rather than an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the tabular presentation with dedicated displays for biological truncation and schedule ablations, protein confidence and diversity, and text generation (Tables 4, 5 and 10–14). All six original figures are retained. Existing tables are repositioned or renumbered, and Table 1's likelihood column becomes App-Log-Lik.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked targeted evidence about its truncation and temperature choices and whether protein reward optimization preserved diversity. v2's ablations and entropy/confidence comparisons substantially strengthen that validation while retaining the original biological results. The stochastic-initialization extension also broadens the supported theoretical scope. The text experiment provides more limited additional support because it measures toxicity reward without evaluating language quality.
